idiom_name: owning handle type with copy/move/destroy hooks (control block for shared ownership, non-owning weak/borrowed view)
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: introduce a handle type that owns the pointee and gives its operations ownership meaning - copy transfers or shares ownership, move transfers it and leaves a valid-but-empty source, destruction releases the object at the last owner. Unique ownership needs no shared state and is the default; shared ownership adds a control block holding strong and weak counts plus the deleter, created exactly once per object. Non-owning views (weak handles, borrowed raw pointers and references) live beside the owning handle and must be promoted or checked before use. Where the language has deterministic scope-exit destruction, tie release to it; where it does not, a documented release protocol plus a scope hook (cleanup attribute, defer, using) takes its place.
code_sketch:
handle h = own(new Body())        # or make_unique/make_shared/Box
use(*h)                          # delegation: the handle acts as the object
other = h                        # share: count += 1  (unique: compile error)
--weak w = observe(h)            # non-owning: does not keep the body alive
if (body := promote(w)) != none: use(*body)
# destruction at the last owner: release once, on every exit path
pitfalls: Two owning handles built from the same raw pointer (two control blocks) destroy the object twice; every owning handle must come from one dedicated allocation or adopt an existing one exactly once.
Shared ownership without a non-owning direction leaks every cycle; the design has to say which edge is weak.
A handle that only looks like a pointer (no ownership transfer on copy) is worse than a raw pointer, because it hides the leak instead of exposing it.

Wrong move: hand out a raw pointer or reference taken with get()/data() from a long-lived owning handle -> failure: the owner is reset, reseated or destroyed while the callee still runs (C++ Core Guidelines R.37), and the borrow silently dangles -> instead: pass the owning handle by value or a weak view down the call chain and take the raw pointer from that local copy.

Wrong move: let an object hand out ownership of itself by building a shared_ptr/Rc from its raw pointer or this -> failure: a second control block is created and the object is destroyed while a user still holds a handle -> instead: derive from enable_shared_from_this (shared_from_this) or keep a Weak self-handle and upgrade() it, so every self-reference comes from the existing control block.
